claims.text: The proposed multiscale simulation will compute phonon and electron thermal transport independently in HfNbTaTiZr.
The simulation will incorporate DFT-derived atomic-disorder and defect-scattering parameters.
The proposed method will reduce prediction error by approximately 30% relative to earlier methods.
The initial alloy is equimolar HfNbTaTiZr.
Experimental HfNbTaTiZr has realistic defect and disorder levels, including a high-temperature variant containing 1 wt.% oxygen.
Below 200 K, lattice and electronic thermal-conductivity contributions in HfNbTaTiZr are comparable and separately measurable.
Impurity scattering and anharmonic effects are significant from 300 to 1200 K.
Atomic-scale disorder and defects, including oxygen-related defects, mediate both phonon and electron scattering.

Separate first-principles parameterization of phonon and electron scattering channels will capture temperature-dependent anharmonicity and impurity effects more accurately than Debye-based or perfect-crystal approaches.
The simulation will produce independent quantitative predictions of lattice and electronic thermal conductivity.
For the oxygen-containing high-temperature specimen, the predicted total thermal conductivity will lie between 10 and 17 W/(K m).
Measurements on HfNbTaTiZr containing 1 wt.% oxygen give total thermal conductivity of 10–17 W/(K m) from 300 to 1200 K.
Earlier approaches use atomic-mass or force-constant variations and DFT-derived elastic properties coupled to analytical estimates requiring a Debye temperature.
Earlier predictive approaches assume perfect, defect-free crystals.
Earlier predictive approaches combine or conflate lattice and electronic transport channels.
The stated accuracy applies only below 200 K and from 300 to 1200 K for samples with approximately 1 wt.% oxygen.
Predictions outside the stated temperature regimes or at substantially different impurity concentrations are uncertain.
Magnetic-field modulation or thermoreflectance can be used to resolve lattice and electronic conductivity independently in the proposed samples.
The hypothesis is falsified if either component has relative prediction error above approximately 30%, or if the high-temperature total prediction falls outside 10–17 W/(K m).
